results.title: A taxonomy for advancing systematic error analysis in multi-site electronic health record-based clinical concept extraction - PMC
results.content: For example, previous studies have found between 4% and 72% f1-score degradation in various domains, such as mental health,3 cardiology,4 and orthopedics.5 Detailed error analysis can systematically study the variation among the clinical language and infer various reasons for heterogeneity factors such as different EHR systems, data quality, clinical practice, and documentation patterns across different institutions. For example, Wu et al developed Errudite, an interactive tool with data grouping functionality to improve the reproducibility and usability of error analysis.6 iSEA is another error analysis pipeline, which automatically discovers semantically-grounded subpopulations with high error rates in the context of a human-in-the-loop interactive system.7 However, in the context of clinical NLP, the process of conducting error analysis can be iterative and complex, requiring both NLP expertise and problem-specific domain knowledge. An iterative taxonomy development process was conducted to create the first version of the taxonomy based on the errors from 2 NLP models (falls and delirium identification) developed by Mayo Clinic and refined on a large corpus to expand coverage. To collect real-world NLP errors, we deployed and ran 2 NLP models (NLP-CAM for delirium-related concept detection23 and NLP-Fall24 for falls detection), which were originally developed at Mayo Clinic Rochester and refined on EHRs from 2 additional health care systems participating in the Rochester Epidemiology Project: (site 1) a network of community-based health systems and a nonprofit community-based clinic and hospital (site 2). In the breast cancer study, the most frequently occurring error types included “Missing\_Annotations,” “Indeterminacy,” and “Absence\_of\_Context.” In the transportation study, common error types included “Missing\_Annotations,” “Exclusion,” and “Status” and for the SDoH study, “Misclassification,” “Absence\_of\_Context,” as well as “Exclusion.” The evaluation also helps identify 2 additional error classes including “Statistical\_Inference” and “Incomplete\_Extraction.” Common examples include rare expression although occurs in training data, the model is still unable to fully capture all possible cases. In our study, we proposed an error taxonomy aimed at accelerating and standardizing the error analysis process in multi-site settings, with the goal of improving the provenance, interpretability, and portability of NLP models. The proposed error taxonomy aims to capture various forms and formats of real-world NLP errors and standardize the error analysis process to provide a unified view of how different NLP models interact with heterogeneous EHR data.

results.title: Data linkage in medical research - PMC
results.content: A barrier to generating linked data that are fit for purpose is the availability of accurate identifiers that can be used to link the same person across multiple data sources.5 Recording of unique identifiers such as the NHS number nearly always involves some degree of error or missing data.6 Therefore, linkage often depends on the use of non-unique identifiers such as name, postcode, and date of birth, or even indirect identifiers such as procedure dates or other clinical variables.7 In combination, these variables can allow us to identify records that belong to the same person—but errors, changes over time, or missing data can still hamper attempts to find the correct link. Several methods can be used to evaluate the quality of linkage.14 These methods focus on identifying potential sources of bias (that is, which characteristics are associated with errors) by examining the characteristics of records that are linked versus unlinked, or that have high versus low quality identifier data, or that are easily identifiable as having been linked incorrectly (eg, through quality control checks).15 Accounting for linkage error in analysis is an ongoing area of methodological research, but includes approaches that view uncertainty in linkage as a missing data problem best handled with some form of multiple imputation or weighting, and those that attempt to quantify and adjust for errors using quantitative bias analysis.16 Reporting guidelines are available that explicitly aim to support transparent reporting of linkage studies.5 17. The biggest barriers to realising the full potential of data linkage as a powerful research tool are gaining and maintaining public trust, and reducing the costs, delays, and inefficiencies in how linked data are made available for research in the public interest.18 19 For example, proposals to routinely link health records in primary and secondary care in order to support planning and research in England (from care.data in 2012 to General Practice Data for Planning and Research in 2021) have repeatedly raised public concerns about the lack of transparency surrounding how linked data are to be used, processes for opting out, and commercial interests.

Due to the high heterogeneity of electronic health record (EHR) settings across different institutions, challenges may arise when attempting to standardize and reproduce the error analysis process. **Objectives:** This study aims to facilitate a collaborative effort to establish common definitions and taxonomies for capturing diverse error types, fostering community consensus on error analysis for clinical concept extraction tasks. **Conclusion:** The proposed taxonomy can facilitate the acceleration and standardization of the error analysis process in multi-site settings, thus improving the provenance, interpretability, and portability of NLP models. **Keywords:** electronic health record; error analysis; natural language processing. results.title: A multi-perspective analysis of retractions in life sciences | Scientometrics
results.content: # A multi-perspective analysis of retractions in life sciences. The aim of this study is to explore trends in retracted publications in life sciences and biomedical sciences over axes like time, countries, journals and impact factors, and topics. Importantly, I employ state-of-the-art analysis and visualization techniques from natural language processing (NLP) to understand the topics in retracted literature. To highlight a few results, the analyses demonstrate an increasing rate of retraction over time and noticeable differences in the publication quality (as measured by journal impact factor) among top countries. The methods and results of this study can be applied to continuously understand the nature and evolution of retractions in life sciences, thus contributing to the health of this research ecosystem. ### Understanding the patterns and magnitude of life science publication Retractions in the last four decades. results.title: What is: Total Error - Understanding Total Error in Data Science
results.content: What is: Total Error - Understanding Total Error in Data Science Click Here to Master Data Analysis! Total Error refers to the cumulative discrepancy between the actual values and the predicted values in statistical analysis and data science. It encompasses all forms of errors that may arise during data collection, processing, and analysis. Understanding Total Error is crucial for data scientists and statisticians as it directly impacts the reliability and validity of their findings. Random error, on the other hand, arises from unpredictable fluctuations in the data collection process, which can lead to variability in the results. By quantifying Total Error, data analysts can identify the extent to which their models deviate from reality, allowing them to make necessary adjustments. Total Error can be calculated using various statistical methods, depending on the context and the type of data involved. Applications of Total Error in Data Science Total Error plays a significant role in various applications within data science, including machine learning, forecasting, and quality control. Strategies to Minimize Total Error To minimize Total Error, data scientists can implement several strategies. These include improving data collection methods to reduce systematic errors, utilizing robust statistical techniques to account for random errors, and continuously validating models against real-world data. Additionally, employing cross-validation techniques can help ensure that models generalize well to unseen data, thereby reducing Total Error. High Total Error can lead to misguided conclusions and poor strategic choices, while low Total Error enhances the credibility of insights derived from data analysis. Organizations that prioritize the reduction of Total Error are better positioned to make informed decisions based on accurate and reliable data. In healthcare, for instance, inaccurate patient data can lead to incorrect diagnoses and treatment plans, highlighting the importance of minimizing Total Error in medical research. Future Trends in Total Error Analysis As data science continues to evolve, the analysis of Total Error is expected to become increasingly sophisticated. Emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, are likely to enhance error detection and correction methods, leading to more accurate data analyses. Furthermore, the integration of real-time data processing will enable organizations to continuously monitor and minimize Total Error, ensuring that their insights remain relevant and actionable.
